L18@P1: The focus of this thesis is on unsupervised learning algorithms, particularly
L19@P1: from the perspective of representation learning. The two main unsupervised
L20@P1: learning methods that we work with are restricted Boltzmann machines and
L21@P1: auto-encoders. Both algorithms are acknowledged to capture meaningful
L22@P1: representations of the data, in which they learn to represent the higher-level
L23@P1: abstractions of the data. In this thesis, the background on unsupervised
L24@P1: learning and the two algorithms are thoroughly discussed using details of
L25@P1: mathematical formulations.
L26@P1: The objective of this thesis is to take the dynamical systems approach
L27@P1: to understand and develop the unsupervised learning models and learning
L28@P1: algorithms through the lens of dynamical systems.
L29@P1: Auto-encoders are perhaps the best-known non-probabilistic methods for
L30@P1: representation learning. They are conceptually simple and easy to train.
L31@P1: Recent theoretical work has shed light on their ability to capture manifold
L32@P1: structure, and drawn connections to density modeling. This has motivated
L33@P1: researchers to seek ways of auto-encoder scoring, which has furthered their
L34@P1: use in classification. Gated auto-encoders (GAEs) are an interesting and
L35@P1: flexible extension of auto-encoders which can learn transformations among
L36@P1: different images or pixel covariances within images. However, they have
L37@P1: been much less studied, theoretically or empirically. For the first part of
L38@P1: our study, we examine the GAEs’s ability to represent different functions or
L39@P1: data distributions. We apply a dynamical systems view to GAEs, deriving a
L40@P1: scoring function, and drawing connections to RBMs. On a set of deep learning
L41@P1-2: iiiii
L42@P2: benchmarks, we also demonstrate their effectiveness for single and multi-label
L43@P2: classification.
L44@P2: Energy-based models are popular in machine learning due to the elegance
L45@P2: of their formulation and their relationship to statistical physics. Among these,
L46@P2: the restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM), and its staple training algorithm
L47@P2: contrastive divergence (CD), have been the prototype for some recent advancements in the unsupervised training of deep neural networks. However, CD has
L48@P2: limited theoretical motivation, and can, in some cases, produce undesirable
L49@P2: behavior. In the second part of our study, we investigate the performance of
L50@P2: Minimum Probability Flow (MPF) learning for training RBMs. Unlike CD,
L51@P2: with its focus on approximating an intractable partition function via Gibbs
L52@P2: sampling, MPF proposes a tractable, consistent, objective function defined in
L53@P2: terms of a Taylor expansion of the KL divergence with respect to sampling
L54@P2: dynamics. We propose a more general form for the sampling dynamics in
L55@P2: MPF, and explore the consequences of different choices for these dynamics
L56@P2: for training RBMs. Experimental results show MPF outperforming CD for
L57@P2-3: various RBM configurations.Contents

L3: # Graham Taylor
L4: 
L5: Professor and Canada Research Chair in Machine Learning. Developing fundamental deep learning methods, with biodiversity science as both motivation and a sandbox for methods at scale.
L6: 
L7: cite2†Scholar†scholar.google.ca cite3†GitHub†github.com cite4†CV Email (gwtaylor@uoguelph.ca)

L9: cite5†Image: Photo of Graham Taylor L10: I lead the Machine Learning Research Group at the University of Guelph. We develop deep learning methods spanning generative modelling, multimodal representation learning across vision, DNA, and language, graph neural networks, and uncertainty quantification — with recurring interests in learning under limited supervision, AI for science, and the design of LLM-based agents as collaborators in research workflows.
L11: Much of this research is motivated by the challenge of monitoring and preserving Earth's biodiversity. With biologists and ecologists, we build large-scale multimodal datasets and foundation models that integrate images, DNA barcodes, and text.
L12: I am a co-PI of cite6†BIOSCAN†bioscan-ml.org , a global initiative monitoring multicellular life at planetary scale, and contribute as senior personnel to the NSF/NSERC-funded cite7†Artificial Intelligence and Biodiversity Change (ABC) Global Center†www.biodiversityai.org , an international team developing AI for ecosystem monitoring.
L13: I co-direct the Centre for Advancing Responsible and Ethical AI (cite8†CARE-AI†www.care-ai.ca ) at Guelph, am a Canada CIFAR AI Chair and faculty member at the cite9†Vector Institute†vectorinstitute.ai , and serve as Academic Director of cite10†Next AI†www.nextcanada.com , a non-profit accelerator for AI-focused entrepreneurs.
